title: Certificates and PKI for endpoints
summary: Understand public key cryptography, X.509 certificates and PKI hierarchy, then deploy and troubleshoot device and user certificates on endpoints using AD CS auto-enrollment, Intune SCEP/PKCS profiles and certutil. You will tie certificates to real endpoint uses such as 802.1X, VPN and certificate-based authentication to Entra.
objectives: Explain asymmetric cryptography and the difference between signing and encryption
Read the key X.509 fields of a certificate and describe what each asserts
Describe a PKI hierarchy with an offline root and issuing CA, and how the chain of trust validates
Trace the certificate lifecycle: enrollment, renewal, and revocation via CRL and OCSP
Deploy device and user certificates to endpoints using AD CS auto-enrollment and Intune SCEP/PKCS profiles
Troubleshoot certificate problems on Windows endpoints using certutil and the certificate stores

quiz.q: A device presents a leaf certificate signed by an issuing CA, which is signed by an offline root CA. What must an endpoint validating this chain have in its trust store for validation to succeed?
options: The root CA certificate installed as a trusted root anchor
A copy of every CRL ever published
quiz.why: Chain validation walks from the leaf up to a self-signed root that must be present and trusted in the LocalMachine\Root (trusted root) store. The intermediate is usually supplied in the chain or AIA; only the root must be pre-trusted as the anchor. Private keys are never distributed for validation.

quiz.q: When a user digitally signs an email with S/MIME, which key performs the signing and which verifies it?
options: Sign with the recipient's public key; verify with the recipient's private key
Sign with the sender's private key; verify with the sender's public key
Sign with a shared symmetric key on both ends
Sign with the CA's private key; verify with the sender's private key
quiz.why: Signing proves origin and integrity, so the sender signs with their own private key and anyone verifies with the sender's public key from the certificate. Encryption is the reverse: you encrypt to the recipient's public key. Mixing these up is the classic PKI exam trap.

quiz.q: An issuing CA is compromised on a Tuesday. Which mechanism lets relying parties learn that previously valid certificates should no longer be trusted, in near real time?
quiz.why: OCSP gives a real-time per-certificate status response and is lighter than downloading a full CRL. The CRL is the periodically published revocation list; OCSP is the live lookup. Auto-enrollment, templates and key archival have nothing to do with revocation distribution.

quiz.q: You are deploying a device certificate to unmanaged-by-domain Windows endpoints via Intune so the private key never leaves the device. Which profile type is the correct choice?
options: SCEP certificate profile with an NDES connector
quiz.why: SCEP has the device generate its own key pair locally and only sends a CSR, so the private key never leaves the endpoint, which is ideal for device authentication. PKCS imported certs are generated centrally (key escrowed) and suit user S/MIME scenarios where the same key must be reused. A trusted root profile only distributes the anchor.

quiz.q: Name the certutil command that displays the certificates currently in a named Windows certificate store, and state which store holds a machine's own identity certificates.
quiz.answer: certutil -store (for example, certutil -store My for the personal/identity store, or certutil -store -enterprise NTAuth). A machine's own identity certificates live in the LocalMachine\My (Personal) store; trusted roots live in LocalMachine\Root.
quiz.why: certutil -store enumerates a store and prints each certificate's subject, serial, thumbprint and whether the private key is present. Knowing My versus Root, and machine versus user scope, is fundamental to triaging endpoint certificate issues.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why a root CA is typically kept offline while an issuing (subordinate) CA stays online.
quiz.answer: The root CA's private key is the ultimate trust anchor, so it is kept offline (powered off or air-gapped) to protect it from compromise, while the online issuing CA does the day-to-day signing and can be revoked and replaced by the root if it is ever breached.
quiz.why: If the root key is stolen the entire PKI collapses and cannot be cheaply recovered, so it signs only the issuing CA(s) and then goes offline; a compromised issuing CA, by contrast, can be revoked by the root and reissued, containing the blast radius.

body_markdown:
## Public key cryptography in two minutes

Everything in PKI rests on **asymmetric cryptography**: a mathematically linked **key pair**. The **private key** is secret and never leaves the holder; the **public key** is freely shared. The two operations matter for endpoints:

- **Signing** proves origin and integrity. You sign with your **private** key; anyone verifies with your **public** key.
- **Encryption** for confidentiality is the reverse. You encrypt to the recipient's **public** key; only their **private** key decrypts.

Getting that direction right is the single most useful thing to internalise.

## What a certificate actually is

A **digital certificate** is a public key plus identity claims, all **signed by a Certificate Authority (CA)**. The format is **X.509**. The fields you will read constantly:

- **Subject** — who the cert identifies (a user, a device, a server FQDN).
- **Issuer** — the CA that signed it.
- **Validity** — not-before and not-after dates.
- **Public key** and **signature algorithm**.
- **Subject Alternative Name (SAN)** — the real identity for TLS and 802.1X.
- **Enhanced Key Usage (EKU)** — what it is allowed to do (Client Authentication, Server Authentication, Code Signing, Secure Email).

## PKI hierarchy and the chain of trust

A production **PKI** is tiered. An **offline root CA** signs one or more **issuing (subordinate) CAs**, then is powered off to protect the ultimate trust anchor. The online **issuing CA** does the everyday signing. An endpoint trusts a leaf certificate only if it can build a chain up to a **root it already trusts** in `LocalMachine\Root`.

```text
Root CA (offline, self-signed)        <- in Trusted Root store
   |  signs
Issuing CA (online, in NTAuth/CA store)
   |  signs
Device / User leaf certificate        <- in LocalMachine\My
```

Validate a chain from a Windows endpoint:

```powershell
# Verify the full chain, revocation and trust path of a cert file
certutil -verify -urlfetch device.cer

# Inspect a CSR before submitting it to the CA
certutil -dump request.req
```

## Lifecycle: enroll, renew, revoke

Certificates are born from a **Certificate Signing Request (CSR)** — the endpoint generates a key pair, keeps the private key, and sends only the public key and subject to the CA. The CA issues against a **template**, the endpoint installs the cert, and **auto-enrollment** in AD CS renews it before expiry. When a cert must be killed early it is **revoked**; relying parties learn this from a periodically published **CRL** or a live **OCSP** lookup.

```text
Key pair generated on device
  -> CSR (public key + subject) sent to CA
  -> CA validates against template, signs, issues
  -> Cert installed in LocalMachine\My (private key stays put)
  -> Auto-enrollment renews before not-after
  -> If compromised: revoke -> appears on CRL / OCSP
```

## Getting certs onto endpoints

Domain-joined devices use **AD CS auto-enrollment** driven by certificate **templates** and Group Policy. For Intune-managed or cloud devices you choose between two profile types: a **SCEP** profile (the device generates its own key, sends a **CSR** via the NDES connector, so the private key never leaves the endpoint — ideal for device auth) or a **PKCS** profile (the key is generated centrally and imported, suited to user **S/MIME** where the same key is reused). A separate **trusted root** profile distributes the anchor. These certs then power **802.1X/Wi-Fi**, **VPN**, **TLS**, **code signing**, **S/MIME**, and **certificate-based authentication to Entra**.

## Troubleshooting with certutil

When authentication fails, certutil is your scalpel. List a store, dump a cert, check the CA-side picture:

```text
certutil -store My                 :: machine identity certs + key presence
certutil -store -user My           :: the user store instead
certutil -store -enterprise NTAuth :: CAs trusted for Entra/AD logon
certutil -dump device.cer          :: decode all X.509 fields
certutil -verify -urlfetch x.cer   :: build chain, fetch CRL/OCSP, report errors
```

The golden questions: is the private key present, does the chain reach a trusted root, has it been revoked, and is the right EKU on it.

## Your task

In a test tenant, deploy a **device certificate** to one managed Windows endpoint using an Intune **SCEP** profile (with its trusted-root and SCEP profiles), then prove it works for **certificate-based authentication**. On the endpoint, run `certutil -store My` and `certutil -verify -urlfetch` against the issued cert, and capture: the Subject, SAN, EKU, the full chain to the root, whether the private key is present, and the revocation check result. Then deliberately revoke the certificate at the CA, force a CRL/OCSP refresh, and document how the endpoint's behaviour changes and what certutil now reports.

slides.title: Certificates and PKI for endpoints
slides.sub: Month 3 - Advanced Endpoint Security & Identity  |  Lesson 6
slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we tackle one of the most powerful and most misunderstood tools in endpoint security: certificates and the public key infrastructure behind them. By the end you'll understand asymmetric keys, what an X point five oh nine certificate really is, how a P K I hierarchy builds a chain of trust, and how to deploy and troubleshoot certificates on real endpoints using certutil and Intune.

slides.title: Asymmetric keys
bullets: A key pair: one private key, one public key.
The private key is secret and never leaves the holder.
The public key is freely shared.
This pairing underpins everything in PKI.
slides.narration: Everything starts with asymmetric cryptography. Instead of one shared secret, you have a key pair: a private key that stays secret and never leaves the holder, and a public key that you hand out freely. The two are mathematically linked, but you cannot derive the private key from the public one. That asymmetry is the foundation of every certificate we'll touch today, so hold onto it.

slides.title: Signing vs encryption
bullets: Sign with your PRIVATE key; verify with your PUBLIC key.
Encrypt to the recipient's PUBLIC key; they decrypt with PRIVATE.
Signing proves origin and integrity.
Encryption provides confidentiality.
slides.narration: Now the single most important distinction. Signing and encryption use the key pair in opposite directions. To sign, you use your own private key, and anyone can verify with your public key. That proves the message came from you and wasn't tampered with. To encrypt to someone, you use their public key, and only their private key can decrypt it. Get this direction right and half of P K I suddenly makes sense.

slides.title: What a certificate is
bullets: A public key plus identity claims, signed by a CA.
The format is X.509.
Key fields: Subject, Issuer, Validity, Public key.
SAN carries the real identity; EKU says what it can do.
slides.code:
Subject:  CN=LAPTOP-7F2A, ...
Issuer:   CN=Contoso Issuing CA
Validity: 2026-01-01 to 2027-01-01
SAN:      DNS=laptop-7f2a.contoso.com
EKU:      Client Authentication (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2)
slides.narration: So what actually is a certificate? It's a public key bundled with identity claims, all signed by a Certificate Authority, a C A. The format is X point five oh nine. You'll read the same fields over and over: the Subject, which is who it identifies; the Issuer, the C A that signed it; the validity dates; the public key itself. And two you must know well: the Subject Alternative Name, the S A N, which carries the real identity for T L S and eight oh two dot one X, and the Enhanced Key Usage, the E K U, which says what the certificate is allowed to do.

slides.title: PKI hierarchy
bullets: Offline root CA is the ultimate trust anchor.
It signs one or more online issuing (subordinate) CAs.
The root is then powered off to protect its key.
Issuing CA does the day-to-day signing.
slides.code:
Root CA (offline, self-signed)
   |  signs
Issuing CA (online)
   |  signs
Device / User leaf certificate
slides.narration: Real P K I is tiered for safety. At the top sits the root C A, which is self-signed and is the ultimate trust anchor. Crucially, after it signs your issuing C As, the root is taken offline, powered off or air-gapped, because if its private key is ever stolen the entire infrastructure collapses. The online issuing, or subordinate, C A then does all the everyday signing. If that issuing C A is compromised, the root can revoke it and you reissue, which contains the damage.

slides.title: Chain of trust
bullets: An endpoint trusts a leaf only if the chain reaches a trusted root.
The root must live in LocalMachine\Root.
Intermediates come via the chain or the AIA extension.
certutil -verify builds and checks the whole path.
slides.narration: Validation works by building a chain. The endpoint takes the leaf certificate, finds its issuer, finds that issuer's issuer, and walks up until it reaches a self-signed root. That root must already be trusted, sitting in the Local Machine Root store. The intermediate issuing C A is usually supplied in the chain or fetched via the A I A extension. To check all of this from a Windows endpoint, certutil dash verify dash urlfetch builds the chain, fetches revocation data and tells you exactly where it breaks.

slides.title: Lifecycle: enroll, renew, revoke
bullets: A CSR carries the public key and subject to the CA.
The private key is generated on, and stays on, the device.
Auto-enrollment renews certs before they expire.
Revocation is published via CRL or checked live via OCSP.
slides.code:
Key pair on device
  -> CSR sent to CA
  -> CA signs against a template
  -> Cert installed; key stays put
  -> Auto-enroll renews; revoke -> CRL/OCSP
slides.narration: Certificates have a lifecycle. They begin with a Certificate Signing Request, a C S R: the device generates a key pair, keeps the private key, and sends only the public key and subject to the C A. The C A issues against a template, and the cert is installed. Auto-enrollment quietly renews it before the not-after date. And when a certificate must be killed early, it's revoked. Relying parties learn that either from a periodically published Certificate Revocation List, the C R L, or from a live O C S P lookup.

slides.title: Deploying certs to endpoints
bullets: Domain devices: AD CS auto-enrollment via templates and GPO.
Intune SCEP: device makes its own key, sends a CSR (key stays).
Intune PKCS: key generated centrally, imported (good for S/MIME).
A trusted root profile distributes the anchor.
slides.narration: How do certs actually land on endpoints? Domain-joined devices use A D C S auto-enrollment, driven by certificate templates and Group Policy. For Intune-managed or cloud devices, you pick between two profiles. A S C E P profile has the device generate its own key and send a C S R through the N D E S connector, so the private key never leaves the endpoint, which is perfect for device authentication. A P K C S profile generates the key centrally and imports it, which suits user S slash M I M E where the same key must be reused. And a separate trusted root profile pushes out the anchor.

slides.title: What endpoint certs are for
bullets: 802.1X / Wi-Fi and wired network authentication.
VPN authentication without passwords.
TLS server identity, S/MIME email, code signing.
Certificate-based authentication to Microsoft Entra.
slides.narration: Why go to all this trouble? Because certificates power so much of the secure endpoint. They authenticate devices onto the network with eight oh two dot one X over Wi-Fi and wired. They authenticate V P N connections without a password to phish. They prove server identity in T L S, sign and encrypt email with S slash M I M E, and sign code so it can be trusted. And increasingly they enable certificate-based authentication straight to Microsoft Entra, giving you genuinely phishing-resistant sign-in.

slides.title: Troubleshooting with certutil
bullets: certutil -store My lists machine identity certs and key presence.
Add -user for the user store; -enterprise NTAuth for logon CAs.
certutil -dump decodes every X.509 field.
Ask: key present? chain to root? revoked? right EKU?
slides.code:
certutil -store My
certutil -store -user My
certutil -store -enterprise NTAuth
certutil -dump device.cer
certutil -verify -urlfetch device.cer
slides.narration: When certificate authentication fails, certutil is your scalpel. certutil dash store My lists the machine's own identity certificates and tells you whether the private key is present. Add dash user to look at the user store instead, or dash enterprise N T Auth to see which C As are trusted for Entra and A D logon. certutil dash dump decodes every X point five oh nine field of a cert file. And the four golden questions to answer every time: is the private key present, does the chain reach a trusted root, has it been revoked, and does it carry the right E K U?

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Sign with private, encrypt to public — never confuse them.
Chain of trust runs leaf -> issuing CA -> offline root.
SCEP keeps the key on the device; PKCS escrows it.
Task: deploy a SCEP device cert, then verify and revoke it.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Asymmetric keys give us signing, with the private key, and encryption, to the public key — never confuse the two. A certificate is a signed public key plus identity, validated by building a chain from the leaf up to an offline root you trust. S C E P keeps the private key on the device while P K C S escrows it centrally. Your task: in a test tenant, deploy a device certificate to one managed Windows endpoint with an Intune S C E P profile, then prove it works for certificate-based authentication. Use certutil dash store My and certutil dash verify dash urlfetch to capture the subject, S A N, E K U, the full chain, whether the key is present, and the revocation result. Then revoke the cert at the C A, refresh the C R L or O C S P, and document exactly how the endpoint's behaviour and certutil's output change. See you in the next lesson.
